\[ \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \left( 2^{-\lfloor 101k/1 \rfloor} + 2^{-\lfloor 101k/2 \rfloor} + \cdots + 2^{-\lfloor 101k/100 \rfloor} \right). \]

Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

message.content:
Let

\[
S=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\sum_{m=1}^{100}2^{-\lfloor 101k/m\rfloor}.
\]

For any integer \(a\ge 1\),

\[
2^{-a}=\sum_{n=a+1}^{\infty}2^{-n}.
\]

Thus, since every floor value is at least \(1\),

\[
S=\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}2^{-n}N_n,
\]

where \(N_n\) is the number of pairs \((k,m)\) with \(k\ge 1\), \(1\le m\le 100\), and

\[
\left\lfloor \frac{101k}{m}\right\rfloor \le n-1.
\]

For fixed \(m\), this condition is equivalent to

\[
\frac{101k}{m}<n \iff k<\frac{mn}{101}.
\]

Hence the number of positive integers \(k\) satisfying it is

\[
\left\lceil \frac{mn}{101}\right\rceil-1.
\]

So

\[
N_n=\sum_{m=1}^{100}\left(\left\lceil \frac{mn}{101}\right\rceil-1\right).
\]

Let \(p=101\). For \(p\mid n\), we have \(\frac{mn}{p}=m\frac np\) integer, so

\[
N_n=\sum_{m=1}^{p-1}\left(m\frac np-1\right)
=\frac np\cdot \frac{p(p-1)}2-(p-1)
=\frac{p-1}{2}(n-2).
\]

If \(p\nmid n\), then \(\frac{mn}{p}\) is not an integer for any \(1\le m\le p-1\), so

\[
\left\lceil \frac{mn}{p}\right\rceil-1
=\left\lfloor \frac{mn}{p}\right\rfloor.
\]

Since \(p=101\) is prime and \(p\nmid n\), the residues \(mn \pmod p\) are exactly \(1,2,\dots,p-1\). Therefore

\[
\sum_{m=1}^{p-1}\left\lfloor \frac{mn}{p}\right\rfloor
=\frac{1}{p}\left(n\sum_{m=1}^{p-1}m-\sum_{m=1}^{p-1}m\right)
=\frac{p-1}{2}(n-1).
\]

Thus, with \(p=101\),

\[
N_n=
\begin{cases}
50(n-1), & 101\nmid n,\\[2mm]
50(n-2), & 101\mid n.
\end{cases}
\]

Therefore

\[
S
=50\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}\frac{n-1}{2^n}
-50\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{2^{101t}}.
\]

Now,

\[
\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}\frac{n-1}{2^n}=1,
\]

and

\[
\sum_{t=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{2^{101t}}
=\frac{1}{2^{101}-1}.
\]

Hence

\[
S=50\left(1-\frac{1}{2^{101}-1}\right)
=\frac{50(2^{101}-2)}{2^{101}-1}.
\]

\[
\boxed{\frac{50(2^{101}-2)}{2^{101}-1}}
\]
